title: Reservation + Paging Sweep: warmup pacing and memory bandwidth postmortem
body:
Summary:

This note summarizes the investigation into an observed 6–9% tail-latency regression in medium-length (512–1024 token) requests when the cluster transitions from a low-load idle period to a sudden burst (traffic ramp). We focused on two interacting subsystems: the lightweight reservation mechanism we introduced last quarter (reservations = short-lived pinned KV residency for expected warmups) and the paging/spill sweep that reclaims memory under pressure. The hypothesis was that reservation lifetime and sweep pacing were interacting with DRAM bandwidth saturation and prefill/warmup patterns to cause transient backpressure and repeated page faults on certain GPUs.

Motivation / Why this matters:
- Customer-facing latency SLOs for chat workloads are sensitive to these transient ramps (PLG teams reported reproducible regressions during demo events).
- Reservations are meant to improve reuse by keeping upcoming KV slices resident; if mis-tuned they can increase eviction churn and page scanning overhead.
- This work aims to produce an actionable tuning and a short-term mitigation for the upcoming Dedicated release patch.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Workload types: (A) synthetic chat traces with 60s idle then 200 req/s burst, (B) mixed-length steady-state baseline, (C) pathological skewed hotset microbench with correlated prefixes.
- Variables: reservation TTL (0ms, 50ms, 200ms, 1s), reservation capacity fraction (0%, 5%, 15%), sweep interval (100ms, 500ms, 2s), sweep work quantum (small/medium/large), prefill strategy (none / eagerly prefill top-5 prefixes / lazy batch prefill).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency, per-GPU DRAM bandwidth (nvprof counters), major page faults, eviction count, reuse-hit ratio, KV residency heatmap (sampling), and CPU scheduler stall events.

Testbed and measurement caveats:
- Tests ran on p4d-family hosts with 80GB GPU memory; cluster configured with multi-tenant allocator identical to prod commit a1b2c3 (same allocator behavior).
- Measurement uses a lightweight agent that samples nvprof counters at 50ms resolution. This under-reports microbursts <50ms.
- We intentionally disabled global background compaction to isolate sweep behavior.

Key findings (high level):
1) Short TTL reservations (50ms) reduced warmup latency for single-request workflows but significantly increased eviction churn in bursts with skewed hotsets. The eviction churn correlated with 10–18% higher DRAM write bandwidth during the burst peak compared to TTL=0ms.
2) Longer TTL (1s) behaved like pinning: reuse improved, but overall resident set growth triggered more frequent sweep cycles; when sweep interval is small (100ms) it created scan thrashing and increased page fault rates by up to 4x on the worst hosts.
3) Sweep work quantum and interval are multiplicative: small interval + large quantum produced the highest CPU idle stalls (driver queueing), while large interval + large quantum caused sudden long pauses when sweeps did run (GC-style stop-the-world effect).
4) Eager prefill of top-5 prefixes with adaptive pacing (rate-limited to match observed DRAM bandwidth headroom) gave the best p95 tail without increasing eviction churn; naive eager prefill without pacing amplified bandwidth spikes and increased p99.
5) When reservation capacity fraction >10% under highly skewed workloads, reuse plateaued while spillback increased — indicating poor marginal utility and raising memory amplification.

Representative data (abbreviated):
- Workload A, burst peak 200 req/s, TTL=50ms, capacity=5%, sweep=500ms, quantum=small:
  p50 18ms / p95 110ms / p99 210ms / eviction_rate +12% / DRAM_write +11%
- Workload A, TTL=0ms, no prefill:
  p50 22ms / p95 140ms / p99 260ms / eviction_rate baseline / DRAM_write baseline
- Workload A, TTL=1s, capacity=15%, sweep=100ms, quantum=large:
  p50 20ms / p95 190ms / p99 420ms / eviction_rate +35% / major_page_faults +3x
- Workload A, TTL=200ms, capacity=5%, sweep=500ms, prefill=adaptive:
  p50 17ms / p95 95ms / p99 180ms / eviction_rate +3% / DRAM_write +3%

Interpretation / root causes (mechanistic):
- Reservation allocation increases transient residency, which is good for reuse, but when multiple reservations overlap in time across tenants the allocator performs extra evictions to make room. Those extra evictions create additional DRAM write traffic (dirty eviction + spill to host memory) and also increase TLB pressure and page table churn.
- The paging sweep is designed to scan candidate pages and reclaim them incrementally. If the sweep interval is too aggressive, it competes with user traffic for PCIe/DRAM bandwidth and driver queues, creating latency spikes. If too lax, the sweep runs as a larger batch and causes stop-the-world latency when it executes.
- Eager prefill without rate limiting replicates the same hit pattern to DRAM as a rush of reservation allocations and hurts tail latency. Adaptive prefill that observes a bandwidth headroom signal prevents that.

Immediate mitigations (short-term, can ship as toggle):
1) Default reservation TTL -> 200ms (was 50ms). Rationale: keeps most short reuse benefits while lowering eviction churn in common burst patterns.
2) Reservation global-cap-percent soft cap -> 10% by default with dynamic decay under observed eviction rate > 15%. Implement a per-pod meter that reduces new reservations when local eviction_rate ramps.
3) Sweep controller: change default sweep interval to 500ms and set quantum to 'small' by default; add jitter to intervals to avoid synchronized cluster-wide sweeps.
4) Prefill: enable adaptive prefill that rate-limits based on a DRAM bandwidth headroom estimator (see prototype in PR 892).
5) Emergency fallback: when observed major_page_faults > threshold (configurable), temporarily disable reservations and trigger a gentle rewarm path (batched async prefill at low rate).

Longer-term changes to explore:
- Reservation bloom filter: keep a lightweight probabilistic filter to avoid creating reservations for prefixes with historically low reuse in the recent epoch. This reduces useless reservation churn for tail prefixes.
- Bandwidth-aware allocator: allocator that reasons about write amplification and defers non-critical dirty evictions to lower-util windows (requires driver/firmware support).
- Per-tenant reservation budgeting tracked across the cluster to prevent multiple tenants from simultaneously consuming reservation capacity in a host-local pocket.
- Page residency heatmap + ML predictor: predict which pages will be reused in the next 500–2000ms window and bias prefill toward those (experimental).

Runbook changes (recommended):
- Add a temporary alert: Elevated eviction rate (>20% over baseline) + DRAM_write delta > 15% for 60s -> Investigate reservation saturation (runbook step: toggle reservation soft-cap to 0% on affected nodes and observe tail latency).
- Add note in SRE runbook to check sweep-config (interval/quantum) after kernel/driver upgrades; driver changes can change the cost model and invalidate our tuned defaults.

Open questions / unresolved bits:
- We saw per-host heterogeneity: some hosts showed no regression even with aggressive settings. Hypothesis: NUMA/PCIe topology differences or local tenant mixing. Need a focused experiment mapping tenant mix to degradation.
- The bandwidth headroom estimator in PR 892 is simple (EWMA). We should evaluate a more robust estimator that accounts for PCIe microbursts and GPU firmware throttling signals.
- Edge case: long-running batched background tasks (compactions) overlapping with burst arrivals produce combinatorial effects; we need to test common background jobs in tandem.

Next steps / action items:
- (Priya) land the sweep interval/quantum defaults change behind a runtime flag; include unit/integration tests for jitter. Target: patch by 2025-03-05.
- (Marco) finish the per-pod eviction rate meter and the soft-cap decay hook. Add telemetry to time-series for 2 weeks. Target: 2025-03-10.
- (Asha) run a tenant-mix experiment matrix on 10 canary hosts to measure host heterogeneity. Target: initial results 2025-03-07.
- (Benji) prototype reservation bloom filter tracer and run simulation against recorded production traces. Target: spike demo 2025-03-14.

Appendix: short checklist for reviewer testing:
- Reproduce with workload A (idle 60s -> burst 200 req/s) on a 4-node canary. Compare p95/p99 with defaults vs our recommended toggles.
- Verify DRAM_write counters on affected nodes; ensure we see the expected reduction.
- Flip reservation soft-cap on a single node during a burst and observe local tail latency.

Notes to self / rough observations:
- The worst offenders were nodes with older driver version 495.x; those showed higher scatter in NVLink transfer times. Worth running upgrade test.
- We should document how reservation metrics appear in the Console (per-route reservation consumption + global soft-cap signal).

If you want reproducer scripts or the raw sampled counter logs, see linked PR and ping me; I dumped the CSVs into the artifact bucket under /artifacts/INF-3427/ (access via internal infra job runner).

-- Priya N.
